The statement fails completely to discuss the many other recreational uses of the public lands that are compatible with environmental protection: hiking, climbing, wildlife watching, nature study, backpacking. These activities have their own "exhilaration" -- a feeling based on a sense of closeness to nature rather than the mechanical thrills of speed and noise. They also bring families together. These other uses are in large measure incompatable with ORV use, because of the noise, smells, environmental destruction and unsightliness of mechanical intrusion. Yet the statement does not give these environmentally preferable uses the consideration they should have on public lands as opposed to ORV use. This makes the impact statement more of an apology for ORV use than a serious analysis of how the environmental values of public lands can be protected from damage.
2. Failure to consider the whole range of possible Departmental restrictions on ORV use which would allow a substantial amount of use without destroying environmental values.
The statement also fails to consider ways in which ORVs can be controlled to preserve the benefits of ORV use without causing serious environmental harm. For example, ORVs could be restricted to tracks, roads, or well-prepared trails, in areas where there is little conflict with environmental values.
